opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer starts with the fact that there's nothing magical about the Riemann hypothesis. It's a hard problem, maybe one of the hardest open problems we have, but in the end a proof is a finite sequence of logical steps. Each step follows from the previous ones according to rules we understand very precisely. So in principle it's a search problem. It's an unimaginably large search space, but it's a search problem, and that's exactly the kind of thing where we've seen AI systems get dramatically better over the last few years.

The second piece is verification. What makes math special compared to almost any other domain is that you can check the answer with complete certainty. At Harmonic we work in Lean, so when the system produces a proof, it's machine-checked. There's no ambiguity about whether it's right. That means you get a perfect reward signal, and you can train on your own outputs without worrying that you're reinforcing subtly wrong reasoning. That's a very different situation from, say, training a model to write essays, where judging quality is fuzzy. In math, you can generate, check, learn, and repeat at enormous scale, and the system keeps getting better.

If you put those together, a well-defined search problem plus a perfect verifier plus a self-improvement loop, I don't see a principled reason why the curve should stop at competition problems or at research problems of moderate difficulty. Human mathematicians are extraordinary, but they have limited time, limited working memory, and they can only explore so many ideas in a career. A system that can explore millions of approaches, learn from every failed attempt, and never lose track of a detail in a hundred-page argument has real structural advantages.

I'll be clear that I'm not saying it's around the corner, or that it'll just be brute force. Something like Riemann will almost certainly require genuinely new mathematical ideas, new definitions, maybe whole new theories, not just clever combinations of existing lemmas. But I think the ability to invent useful abstractions is also something these systems can learn, because you can measure whether an abstraction actually helps you prove things. So when people ask whether an AI could solve Riemann, my view is that it's a question of when, not if. And honestly, if we build something that can't eventually get there, I'd consider that we haven't really built mathematical superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response argues AI should eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis and does not identify proving it undecidable as a worthwhile alternative.

r002.rationale: It says a proof may require new ideas, definitions, or theories, but does not explain that leading mathematicians create theories by connecting existing mathematical results.

r003.rationale: It describes AI search, verification, and learning, but does not say the system mirrors leading mathematicians’ process of synthesizing frontier results.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest framing is that it's not that any one specific problem should be solvable on day one. It's that if you're building a math system and it can't, in principle, be aimed at something like the Riemann hypothesis, then you've built the wrong thing.

Here's how I think about it. Mathematics is unusual among domains because it's fully verifiable. If you write a proof in a formal language like Lean, a checker can tell you with certainty whether it's correct. There's no ambiguity, no human in the loop needed to judge quality. That means you can run the search for a very long time, generate huge numbers of candidate ideas, and throw away everything that doesn't check out, without accumulating errors. Most of what makes AI unreliable in other fields just doesn't apply.

So once you have that loop working, the question becomes purely one of scale and search. How much compute do you point at a problem, and how smart is the system at proposing the next lemma, the next construction, the next intermediate result. Riemann is hard because the path to it is long and probably goes through mathematics that doesn't exist yet. But "long path through new territory" is exactly what a system that can verify every step and never gets tired is suited for. Humans have had 160 years, and the bottleneck has been that very few people can hold the right ideas in their head at once and sustain the effort.

The other piece is that these systems are already doing real research-level mathematics. Not the Riemann hypothesis, obviously, but open problems, things that working mathematicians cared about and hadn't resolved. And the gap between "solves a problem no one had solved" and "solves a famous problem no one had solved" is mostly a matter of depth, not of kind.

I don't want to overclaim the timeline. But I think if you don't believe the trajectory ends with something like Riemann, you have to explain what stops it. And I've never heard a convincing answer to that.

r002.rationale: It says the path may require new mathematics and intermediate results, but does not explain that leading mathematicians create theories by connecting existing results.

r003.rationale: It describes AI proposing lemmas and constructions, but does not state that the system mirrors leading mathematicians’ process of synthesizing frontier results.

astra-6.text:
I think the Riemann hypothesis is a useful example because it’s a problem where we don’t know what the solution will look like. You can’t just reproduce a proof someone has already written. You have to come up with new ideas, explore them, and figure out which ones actually work.

If we want AI systems that can do research, that’s the kind of capability we’re aiming for. There’s nothing about mathematics that suggests the discoveries humans can make are the limit of what’s possible. So I wouldn’t claim that solving the Riemann hypothesis is imminent, but I also don’t see a principled reason an AI system couldn’t do it. The challenge is building a system that can make sustained progress on something genuinely new.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Riemann hypothesis is a useful way to make the ambition concrete. We want a system that can do original mathematics, not just reproduce proofs of things people already know. So, in principle, it should be able to explore ideas, develop new tools, and put them together into a proof that nobody has seen before.

That doesn’t mean I know when it will solve the Riemann hypothesis, or that it’s the first problem we should aim at. But if there’s a proof that humans could discover, I don’t see a fundamental reason an AI system couldn’t discover it too. The challenge is building something that can sustain that kind of reasoning and reliably check its own work.
